points.en: Gives a clear subject and plural keyword that unite the points, such as 'necessities in prayer'.
Rewrites each point as a particular instance of the keyword, such as the need to request, to praise and to confess.
Removes the vague 'some other remarks' point and the point that did not concern prayer.
Gives three points that are each a distinct reason to forgive, all fitting the subject.
The points are parallel in grammatical form and use active verbs.
Gives a Scripture reference supporting each point.
Parallelism is broken: the points mix full sentences, a phrase and a single word.
Order and unity are weak: points overlap with each other and with the first point, repeating the same idea instead of staying distinct.
Rewrites the outline with distinct points in parallel form.
Outlines the seven words of the cross in order: pardon, promise, provision, pain, dereliction, triumph, commitment.
Cites the verse for each of the seven words.
Notes that seven points exceed the normal range of two to five (three as the usual default).
Explains that subpoints are dropped when a sermon has more than three points.
The preacher's authority is the Word of God, so he may make only the points Scripture itself supports.
Without a supporting verse a point is the preacher's own idea, and he has stepped outside that authority.
Such preaching becomes opinion or moralism dressed in Biblical language.
Deductive outline: states a general subject (such as reasons the Lord is my Shepherd) and lists specific, parallel points with Scripture.
Inductive outline: lists specific images from the Psalm and moves toward a general truth at the end.
Says which method fits Psalm 23 better and gives a reason.
Addresses the meditative, image-by-image character of the Psalm.
Unity: all three points are acts of compassion, instances of one subject.
Parallelism: each point uses the same active form (He healed, He loved, He fed).
Suggests a real improvement, such as reordering for movement (strongest first, most evangelistic last) or adding a verse to each point.
Proportion: the points are short and roughly equal.
The diagnosis is a failure of proportion: one point swallows the sermon while the others are rushed, the tail wagging the dog.
He should plan and cut so that each division gets roughly equal development.
A point important enough to make deserves development; one that cannot be developed may not be a separate point.
Deduction reasons from the general to the specific: state a general truth, then list specific instances of it.
Induction is the reverse: it begins with the specific and moves to the general.
Sketches three parallel points that break 'God is faithful' into specific ways it is true.
Gives a Scripture reference supporting each point.
Names at least three of the five marks (unity, order, movement, proportion, parallelism) and says what each means.
Applies the marks to a specific sermon, not a generic description.
Judges honestly whether the sermon met each mark, including weaknesses.
